segments.narration: A man jumped from a jet with $200,000 cash. November 24th, 1971, somewhere over southwest Washington, in the dark.
He bought a ticket as Dan Cooper. Handed a note to a flight attendant, asked for four parachutes and ten thousand twenty-dollar bills.
Passengers released in Seattle. Then he lowered the rear airstair mid-flight and stepped out. The crew felt the tail pitch up at 8:13.
How do you disappear carrying a sack of recorded serial numbers? For eight years, not one bill surfaced anywhere.

February 1980: an eight-year-old found three rotting packets on the Columbia River, six thousand dollars. The FBI shelved the case in 2016; its own agent had already concluded Cooper never survived the jump.

verdicts.claim: The hijacker used the alias Dan Cooper, passed a note to a flight attendant, and demanded four parachutes and $200,000 in 10,000 unmarked twenty-dollar bills.
verdicts.note: 80% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: After the passengers were released in Seattle, Cooper lowered the aft airstair in flight and the crew felt the tail pitch up at about 8:13 pm.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: last crew contact around 8:00 pm, tail section pitched upward around 8:13 pm.

verdicts.claim: None of the ransom money was recovered for more than eight years after the hijacking.
verdicts.note: 70% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: In February 1980 eight-year-old Brian Ingram found three packets of the ransom totalling about $6,000 on the Columbia River at Tena Bar; the FBI suspended active investigation on 8 July 2016, and its case agent concluded in 2007 that Cooper most likely did not survive the jump.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives 10 February 1980, Brian Ingram, aged eight, three packets totalling $6,000; the 8 July 2016 suspension; and Larry Carr's 2007 conclusion. Press reports put the recovered sum at about $5,800, so the narration says 'six thousand dollars' as the rounded figure Wikipedia gives.
